questions.q: What is the core distinguishing factor between HA and DR, per this lesson?
options: Scope of failure — HA covers local, component-level failures; DR covers loss of an entire site
HA and DR are interchangeable terms for the same thing
HA is for cloud databases and DR is only for on-prem databases
DR always recovers faster than HA
questions.explain: HA addresses a narrow, local failure with fast automatic recovery; DR addresses losing a whole site and requires a physically separate location.

questions.q: Why do DR technologies tolerate more latency and asynchronous behavior than HA technologies?
options: Because the secondary site is physically distant, so network latency makes synchronous behavior impractical
Because DR technologies don't actually replicate any data
Because DR is only used for non-critical databases
Because asynchronous replication is always more accurate than synchronous
questions.explain: Physical distance between the primary and DR site introduces latency that makes strict synchronous commit impractical, so DR designs favor asynchronous replication.

questions.q: According to this lesson, why is a Failover Cluster Instance (FCI) considered pure HA rather than DR?
options: Because all FCI nodes share the same storage, typically in one datacenter — the whole cluster fails if that storage is destroyed
Because FCI cannot fail over automatically
Because FCI only works in the cloud
Because FCI replicates data to a second datacenter automatically
questions.explain: FCI nodes share storage, so it protects against a node failing but not against loss of the shared storage or the site itself.

questions.q: How can a single Availability Group serve both HA and DR at once?
options: By having a local synchronous replica for HA and a remote asynchronous replica in another datacenter for DR
By running two separate SQL Server instances that never communicate
AGs can never serve both HA and DR — this is impossible
By using FCI instead of AG for the remote replica
questions.explain: A stretched AG topology combines a fast local synchronous replica (HA) with a distant asynchronous replica (DR) under one technology.

questions.q: An FCI protects a SQL Server against node failure, but all nodes share one SAN in a single datacenter. What real event would this configuration fail to protect against?
options: A site-wide disaster (like a fire or flood) that destroys the shared SAN or the datacenter itself
A single node's CPU failing
A single node's network card failing
Nothing — this configuration protects against every possible failure
questions.explain: Because all FCI nodes depend on the same shared storage in one location, a site-wide disaster takes out the entire cluster at once — this is a DR gap, not an HA one.
